learn: The first people in the Americas arrived many thousands of years ago, probably crossing from Asia.
Native American nations developed diverse cultures adapted to their environments: the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) in the Northeast, the Pueblo in the Southwest, the Lakota on the Plains.
The Haudenosaunee Confederacy united six nations under a shared constitution, the Great Law of Peace.
check: Native cultures were adapted to their...
lessons.try: Make a chart of four Native American nations and how they adapted to their region.

learn: Spain explored and conquered much of the Americas, building missions and colonies.
France explored the St. Lawrence and Mississippi rivers and traded furs with Native nations.
Exploration brought disease and conflict to Native peoples.
lessons.try: Trace Spanish and French exploration routes on a map.

learn: Jamestown, Virginia (1607), was the first permanent English settlement.
Tobacco became its cash crop; the Powhatan people helped and then resisted the settlers.
The Pilgrims founded Plymouth in 1620 and signed the Mayflower Compact.
check: The Mayflower Compact was an early form of...
lessons.try: Read the Mayflower Compact and explain its idea of self-government.

learn: New England (Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, New Hampshire) had rocky soil and cold winters.
Economies relied on fishing, shipbuilding and trade.
Town meetings let citizens make local decisions.
check: An important New England industry was...
lessons.try: Compare life in a New England town with your town.

learn: The Middle Colonies (New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware) were "breadbasket" colonies with diverse populations.
Pennsylvania, founded by William Penn, offered religious freedom.
The Southern Colonies grew tobacco, rice and indigo on plantations worked by enslaved Africans.
lessons.try: Make a map showing the three colonial regions and their economies.

learn: Colonies developed representative assemblies like Virginia's House of Burgesses (1619).
Enslaved Africans were brought to the colonies beginning in 1619 and denied all rights.
Enslaved people resisted in many ways and kept their cultures alive.
check: The House of Burgesses was in...
The House of Burgesses began in...
lessons.try: Research the Middle Passage and write a reflection.

learn: Britain and France fought for control of North America (1754-1763).
Britain won but was left with huge debts.
To pay, Britain taxed the colonies.
check: The French and Indian War ended in...
Britain tried to pay debts by...
lessons.try: Explain how winning the war led to new problems.

learn: The Stamp Act (1765) taxed printed materials; colonists protested "No taxation without representation."
The Townshend Acts taxed imports; colonists boycotted British goods.
In the Boston Tea Party (1773), colonists dumped British tea into the harbour.
check: The Boston Tea Party was in...
lessons.try: Write a protest pamphlet against the Stamp Act.

learn: The Boston Massacre (1770) killed five colonists.
Britain passed the Intolerable Acts to punish Massachusetts.
The First Continental Congress met in 1774 to respond.
check: The First Continental Congress met in...
lessons.try: Make a timeline from 1763 to 1775.

learn: Fighting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775.
Thomas Paine's "Common Sense" (1776) argued for independence.
The Declaration of Independence, written mainly by Thomas Jefferson, was adopted on July 4, 1776.
lessons.try: Read the Declaration's preamble and explain its main ideas.

learn: George Washington led the Continental Army.
The victory at Saratoga (1777) convinced France to join the American side.
Washington's troops survived a harsh winter at Valley Forge.
check: The Continental Army was led by...
Valley Forge is known for a harsh...
lessons.try: Map five key battles of the Revolution.

learn: The British surrendered at Yorktown in 1781.
The Treaty of Paris (1783) recognised American independence.
Many groups, including women, enslaved people and Native Americans, did not gain equal rights.
check: The Treaty of Paris was signed in...
lessons.try: Discuss who gained and who didn't from independence.

learn: The first US government under the Articles of Confederation was weak.
Congress couldn't tax, raise an army easily or regulate trade.
Shays' Rebellion (1786) showed the need for a stronger government.
check: The Articles of Confederation created a ___ government.
lessons.try: List the weaknesses of the Articles.

learn: Delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787 to write a new constitution.
The Great Compromise created a Senate (equal votes) and a House (based on population).
The Three-Fifths Compromise counted enslaved people as three-fifths of a person for representation, a deeply unjust bargain.
lessons.try: Role-play the debate between large and small states.

lessons.t: Ratification and the Bill of Rights
learn: Federalists supported the Constitution; Anti-Federalists feared a strong government.
The Federalist Papers, by Hamilton, Madison and Jay, argued for ratification.
The Bill of Rights (1791), the first ten amendments, protected individual freedoms.
check: The Bill of Rights is the first ___ amendments.
The First Amendment protects freedom of...
lessons.try: Rank the five freedoms of the First Amendment by importance to you.

learn: Popular sovereignty: power comes from the people ("We the People").
Limited government: the government can do only what the Constitution allows.
Federalism divides power between national and state governments.
check: Dividing power between nation and states is...
lessons.try: Find examples of federal and state powers.

lessons.t: Separation of Powers and Checks and Balances
learn: The legislative branch (Congress) makes laws; the executive (President) enforces them; the judicial (courts) interprets them.
Checks and balances let each branch limit the others: the President can veto, Congress can override, courts can rule laws unconstitutional.
This prevents any branch from becoming too powerful.
lessons.try: Make a diagram of the three branches and their checks.

learn: The Constitution can be amended; 27 amendments have been added.
Citizens have rights and responsibilities: voting, jury duty, obeying laws, staying informed.
The 13th, 14th, 15th and 19th Amendments expanded freedom and voting rights.
lessons.try: Research an amendment and explain its impact.

learn: George Washington became the first President in 1789 and set precedents like the Cabinet.
His Farewell Address warned against political parties and foreign alliances.
John Adams was the second President; political parties formed in his time.
check: The first President took office in...
lessons.try: Read part of Washington's Farewell Address.

learn: Thomas Jefferson bought the Louisiana Territory from France in 1803, doubling the nation's size.
Lewis and Clark explored it with the help of Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman.
Marbury v. Madison (1803) established judicial review.
lessons.try: Trace Lewis and Clark's route.

lessons.t: The War of 1812 and Monroe Doctrine
learn: The War of 1812 with Britain ended in a draw but boosted national pride.
"The Star-Spangled Banner" was written during the war by Francis Scott Key.
The Monroe Doctrine (1823) warned Europe not to colonise the Americas further.
check: The War of 1812 was fought against...
lessons.try: Explain why the War of 1812 is sometimes called the "Second War of Independence".

learn: Manifest Destiny was the belief that the US should expand across the continent.
Settlers moved west on the Oregon Trail; the US gained Texas and the Southwest after war with Mexico (1846-1848).
The California Gold Rush (1849) brought thousands west.
check: Manifest Destiny was the belief in...
The war with Mexico ended in...
lessons.try: Map how the US grew between 1800 and 1850.

learn: The Indian Removal Act (1830), signed by Andrew Jackson, forced Native nations west.
The Cherokee were forced to march west on the Trail of Tears (1838-1839); thousands died.
This was a grave injustice that Native nations still remember.
check: The Indian Removal Act was signed by...
The Trail of Tears forced the ___ west.
The Trail of Tears was in...
lessons.try: Read a Cherokee account of removal.

learn: Abolitionists like Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman fought to end slavery.
The Seneca Falls Convention (1848) began the women's rights movement.
Reformers also worked for public schools and better treatment of the mentally ill.
check: The women's rights movement began at...
Harriet Tubman led people on the...
lessons.try: Research a reformer and present their work.

units.t: Slavery, Sectionalism and the Civil War

learn: The North industrialised; the South depended on cotton and slavery.
Compromises (1820, 1850) tried to balance free and slave states.
The Dred Scott decision (1857) ruled enslaved people were not citizens, deepening the divide.
check: The Dred Scott decision was in...
lessons.try: Make a chart comparing the North and South.

learn: After Abraham Lincoln's election in 1860, Southern states seceded and formed the Confederacy.
The war began at Fort Sumter in 1861.
Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation (1863) declared enslaved people in rebel states free.
lessons.try: Read the Gettysburg Address and explain its message.

learn: Gettysburg (1863) was a turning point.
The war ended at Appomattox in 1865; Lincoln was assassinated days later.
About 620,000 soldiers died.
lessons.try: Make a timeline of the Civil War.

learn: Reconstruction (1865-1877) aimed to rebuild the South and reunite the nation.
The Freedmen's Bureau helped formerly enslaved people with schools, food and jobs.
Black Americans built churches, schools and communities.
lessons.try: Research a school founded during Reconstruction.

learn: The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery.
The 14th (1868) granted citizenship and equal protection.
The 15th (1870) protected Black men's right to vote.
lessons.try: Explain each amendment in your own words.

learn: Reconstruction ended in 1877 when federal troops left the South.
Southern states passed "Jim Crow" laws enforcing segregation and blocking Black voters.
The struggle for civil rights continued for another century.
check: The civil rights struggle continued for...
lessons.try: Discuss how the end of Reconstruction affected Black Americans.
